newsitem.title: UK: Oil markets rebound ahead of key U.S. stocks data.
newsitem.headline: Oil markets rebound ahead of key U.S. stocks data.

text.p: Oil markets rebounded on a technical correction after a nearly 10 percent drop in the last two weeks and ahead of a key industry report on U.S. inventories, traders said.

March futures for world benchmark Brent Blend crude rose to an intra-day high of $22.80 a barrel, a gain of 44 cents, before being knocked down by technical selling on the New York market during the afternoon session.
At 1634 GMT, Brent was trading at $22.32 a barrel, down three cents. ent Blend crude gained 21 cents to $22.57 a barrel.
"I think that with gas oil getting down toward the $200 mark and prompt Brent not far from $22, it starts to look a little bit cheap," said Tony Machacek, an oil broker at Credit Lyonnais Rouse.
"A lot of the speculators may not want to sell near those numbers because the potential to go much below them...is a bit limited considering there isn't a massive change in fundamentals," he said.
Those fundamentals, including the weather, may keep oil prices volatile as the industry meets demand for home heating oil with an eye to stepping up gasoline output before the spring driving season.
Record cold weather in Europe earlier this month was replaced by an Arctic blast that ripped across the U.S. Midwest and the Northeast, which is the world's largest heating oil market.
But some predicted the peak in heating oil demand may be near at hand. The spot gas oil contract in London has come down to $203 a tonne from $235 in early January.
"The market is a mixed bag of tricks," said Jeff Potter, managing director of Dublin-based Univest Ireland Ltd.
"A lot of this is technical. We had one of the coldest days of the year last week and the market dropped sharply," he said. "Some of the contracts look good and some of the contracts look bad."

American Petroleum Institute (API) weekly data on U.S. stock movements are due out after the close of business on Wednesday and may offer the next clue to price direction. The report was delayed one day because of the U.S. Martin Luther King holiday.
Gasoline inventories were nearly 10 million barrels below a year ago last week while distillates (which including heating oil) have crept up to levels close to last winter.
"It may be a bit of a psychological factor if you start to see distillate stocks above this time last year...but a lot of that bearish sentiment is probably factored in," Machahek said.
"Stocks of gasoline are relatively low and it looks as though we're going to have a fairly good turnaround season," he said.
Refineries typically shut down some operations near the end of winter to switch over to producing more gasoline for the warmer weather.
Also clouding the market has been a sharp rise in the U.S. dollar. This has discouraged buying of heating oil in Germany, the biggest market in Europe.
German consumers, who pay in marks for the fuel, have limited their purchases since last summer, keeping inventories just above 55 percent of capacity and leaving them vulnerable to the cold weather.
"The market will pick up again," one German trader said. "At such low (stock) levels, you have to buy. If you need, you need, whatever the cost."
